clue.text: Book about two pintos?

parts.note: a quart holds two pints, so tacking an O on, as 'pints' becomes 'pintos', turns that measure into a size of book made by folding sheets twice

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is outrageous: 'pintos' is not about horses or beans but is 'pints' with an O added, and the book size is the two-pint measure with the same O on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A book in this format has pages made by folding a printed sheet twice, giving four leaves.

clue.text: Time for mercy, when rent's due?

parts.note: quarter is mercy shown to a beaten enemy, as in give no quarter
a day is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone asks when leniency might be shown to a tenant behind on payments.
explanation.walkthrough: The four English days marking the start of each quarter of the year were when rents traditionally fell due.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional English rent and tenancy payments fell due on these four dates each year.

clue.text: Mouth open for feast

definitions.meaning: with jaw dropped, gaping in wonder
an early Christian love feast or communal meal

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means gaping in astonishment; the Greek noun names a communal meal of fellowship.

clue.text: Deceive a couple on newspaper? Not quite

parts.note: a couple is two

indicators.note: not quite means the word for the newspaper is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: The Times is a newspaper

explanation.surface: A tabloid nearly exposes a couple's deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' drops the final S of TIMES; 'on' places one piece above the other in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To be unfaithful to a partner by seeing someone else is to deceive them.

clue.text: Early version of film showing hooligan use razor

parts.note: a rough is a thug or hooligan
to cut is what you do when you use a razor

explanation.surface: A film shows a yob wielding a razor.
explanation.definitionFit: Editors assemble a preliminary edit of a film before refining it into the final version.

clue.text: River creature gets over keeping dry S U

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the word for over holds the word for dry

parts.note: o'er is a poetic contraction of over
TT, teetotal, means abstaining from drink, that is dry

explanation.surface: An aquatic animal climbs out and stays dry.
explanation.walkthrough: The poetic contraction for over is the key piece here; the trailing 'S U' is the count misread in printing, and 'gets' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: This playful fish-eating mammal lives in and beside rivers.

clue.text: Uphill through barrier needs throttle

indicators.note: through means passing inside, so the reversed hill goes inside the barrier

parts.note: a gate is a barrier

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for hill is read from the bottom

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Climbing a hill past a barrier leaves one gasping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uphill' reads as one word but splits: 'Up' reverses the hill in this down clue, and 'through' puts that inside the barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to strangle someone, especially with a cord or wire.

clue.text: No inclination from the military to make allowance for royalty

definitions.meaning: a lean or tilt that is civilian rather than military, read literally
the annual sum voted by Parliament for the monarch's household

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is literal: civil means not military, and a list is a tilt or lean, as a ship lists.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament votes this yearly grant to cover the British sovereign's official expenses.

clue.text: I left apple, say, rolling over in grass

indicators.note: rolling over turns the shortened word to read the other way
left means gone, so the I is removed from the word for apple

parts.note: an apple is an example of fruit

explanation.surface: An apple rolls away across the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' takes I out of FRUIT, giving FRUT, and 'rolling over' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: Sod or grassy lawn cut into squares is a word for grass-covered ground.

clue.text: Castle's shade over mature lake

parts.note: a tint is a shade of colour
to age is to mature
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A castle's colour has mellowed beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' places TINT above AGE in this down clue; the 's of Castle's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: This ruined Cornish fortress on the coast is linked in legend with King Arthur.

clue.text: Structural expert rebuilt a station across motorway

indicators.note: the rearranged letters stretch across, that is either side of, the motorway letter
something rebuilt is put together again in a new form, so the letters of a station are rearranged

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: An engineer reconstructs a railway station spanning a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebuilt' turns A STATION into ANATOIST, and 'across' puts M inside it. The surface engineer is really someone who studies the body's structure.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientist of anatomy studies the bodily structure of living things.

clue.text: Runs ended, one in Bristol, one in Doncaster, perhaps

definitions.text: one in Bristol, one in Doncaster, perhaps

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
something that has ended is over

explanation.surface: A cricket score report ends with runs, mentioning players in two English towns.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol Rovers and Doncaster Rovers are English football clubs, so a player for either is one of these. 'Runs' tempts towards a river; the clubs kill it.
explanation.definitionFit: Each club's players share the club's nickname, so a single player is named in the singular after it.

clue.text: Play we halt, interest failing

indicators.note: failing suggests falling apart, so the letters of we halt and interest collapse into a new order

explanation.surface: A theatre company stops a performance because the audience is losing interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing' signals that WE HALT INTEREST is rearranged into the fourteen letters of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: This late romance by Shakespeare, set in Sicily and Bohemia, is a stage drama.

clue.text: Keep visiting northern France, seeing surf from one's seat

definitions.meaning: repeatedly crossing to the French coast, as on booze cruises
zapping between TV programmes with the remote, never leaving the armchair

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means making frequent trips across the English Channel, or flicking between TV stations.

clue.text: Chap in gallery has non-British accent

indicators.note: non-British asks for the B, the abbreviation for British, to be taken away

parts.note: a brogue is a regional accent, especially Irish

explanation.surface: A man in an art gallery speaks with a foreign accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'gallery' is a rogues' gallery, the police collection of photos of criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogues' gallery is a set of mugshots, so a fellow pictured in it is a scoundrel.

clue.text: Went like a lamb, but risked speaking Check to

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Went like a lamb, but risked speaking Check to': 'Check to' fits no parse and the scan and blog do not show the rest; the homophone of gambled is clear.
annotationWithheld.clue: Went like a lamb, but risked speaking Check to

clue.text: Sigh horribly about liar — not the first to produce nonsense

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round, about, the shortened liar
horribly suggests something done badly, so the letters of sigh are jumbled
the first letter of the word for a liar is dropped

parts.note: a fibber tells lies

explanation.surface: Someone sighs in frustration at a liar talking rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sigh is fodder, not a mood; 'horribly' shuffles it into two parts that sit either side of the trimmed liar.
explanation.definitionFit: Unintelligible babble or meaningless talk is a common synonym for nonsense.

clue.text: Looking healthy and prosperous, bank-minute, ing pounds

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Looking healthy and prosperous, bank-minute, ing pounds': the middle is garbled OCR, and neither the scan nor a search recovers the wording.
annotationWithheld.clue: Looking healthy and prosperous, bank-minute, ing pounds

clue.text: In a stream, see crazy old animal

indicators.note: In tells us crazy is to be placed inside a stream

parts.note: a rill is a small stream
mad means crazy

explanation.surface: Someone sees something odd and ancient in a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts MAD inside A RILL, after its R, and the abbreviation O is added at the end; 'see' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: This armoured burrowing mammal of the Americas is a kind of creature.

clue.text: Sort of radio knob absorbing silly chap

indicators.note: absorbing means taking in, so the knob takes in the silly chap

parts.note: a dial is a knob on a radio
a git is a contemptible or silly man, British slang

explanation.surface: A radio's tuning knob attracts an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: GIT is British slang for a foolish or unpleasant man.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasting by encoded signals rather than analogue waves describes a kind of radio.

clue.text: Joy keeps to bed

indicators.note: keeps means holds inside, so the word to is held within the word for joy

parts.note: fun is enjoyment or joy

explanation.surface: Happiness stays with someone who goes to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese-style mattress, often on a low frame, serves as a sofa or a place to sleep.

clue.text: Potter thus leading conspiracy

definitions.meaning: a snooker player who pots balls and is ahead by one game
a plot to make an innocent person appear guilty

explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' is a snooker player, not a pottery maker or Harry Potter; a snooker game is a frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot to incriminate an innocent person is a kind of conspiracy.

clue.text: Why we calibrate scales, as finishing touch?

definitions.meaning: scales are set accurately so that shoppers receive a fair weight, read literally
an idiom for something added as an extra on top of what is needed

explanation.surface: Someone explains why shopkeepers check their scales, and wonders about a final flourish.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means as a bonus beyond what is strictly required; literally it describes the reason for accurate weighing.

clue.text: Different theory almost worked

indicators.note: worked means kneaded or reshaped, so the remaining letters are rearranged
almost means the word theory is cut short, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A distinct hypothesis nearly succeeded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims THEORY to THEOR, and 'worked' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something distinct or not the same is a synonym for different.

clue.text: Wedding could be seen in middle of Grand Canal

definitions.meaning: a marriage, a joining of two people

definitions.text: could be seen in middle of Grand Canal
definitions.meaning: the word fills the gap in the name of England's longest canal, the Grand ... Canal

explanation.walkthrough: The Grand Union Canal links London and Birmingham, so the word sits in the middle of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A marriage joins two people, so the word for joining means a wedding.

clue.text: Ducks out of greeting, being in a state

indicators.note: out of here means outside, so the ducks sit either side of the greeting

parts.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so two ducks are two O's
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: Ducks dodge a greeting while in a fluster.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a score of zero, so it gives O. 'being in' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: This Midwestern US state lies south of Lake Erie.

clue.text: He's no-good pilot? He's bound to land

parts.note: taken as the word he, the 's not giving a letter

indicators.note: no-good asks for PI, the crossword abbreviation for pious or good, to be removed

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a poor pilot is doomed to crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no-good' removes PI from PILOT, leaving LOT. The definition is not about a crash: a serf is legally bound to the land he works.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Sparta this class of serfs was tied to the land and owned by the state.

clue.text: Suggest about half hour for his music

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for suggest goes round the word for half

parts.note: to hint is to suggest
demi is a prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: Someone hints at about half an hour of music.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works by naming the composer whose works are 'his music'.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Hindemith was a twentieth-century German composer, so his name stands for his body of compositions.

clue.text: Scruffy gold parrot is standard

indicators.note: scruffy means untidy and messed up, so the letters of gold are disordered

parts.note: a lory is a brightly coloured Australasian parrot

explanation.surface: A tatty golden parrot is described as normal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scruffy' makes OLDG from GOLD. 'standard' here means a flag, not normal.
explanation.definitionFit: This nickname for the US Stars and Stripes is a flag, and a flag is also called a standard.

clue.text: Protected by publisher, writer is to speak his heart

indicators.note: protected by means surrounded, so the writer goes inside the publisher

parts.note: OUP is Oxford University Press, a publisher
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A writer shielded by his publisher must reveal his feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: OUP, Oxford University Press, is a crossword stalwart for publisher; 'Protected by' wraps it round the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: To unburden oneself and talk frankly about feelings is an idiom for confiding everything.
